mvpAdversarialAudit.notes: Endorsements were abundant and clear in the back third: INT004 responded enthusiastically to the rebuild-tracking executive assistant concept (cues 241, 244–245, 347–349), the community intelligence and advocacy summary layer (cue 300), and the context-aware personalized bot (cue 310). The contractor bid comparison idea (cues 367–382, 399–400) was the single most animated and elaborated moment in the entire demo section. For hesitations: his one clear hesitation was a lukewarm, hedged response to the box-breathing anxiety demo ('I haven't tried it, so…', cue 335) — not rejection, but withheld judgment pending direct experience. His broader AI skepticism ('I haven't noticed its efficacy compared to all the hype around it', cue 214) was expressed before the demo began and is coded as aiAttitudesAndBeliefs, not mvpFeedback. During the demo itself, no concerns about accuracy, privacy, or emotional dependency were raised. The only hesitation is the measured neutrality toward the emotional support component.

summary:
INT004 is a 47-year-old male Eaton Fire survivor whose home was completely destroyed. He and his wife relocated to a nearby apartment quickly after the fire and have maintained as much of their pre-fire routine as possible. At 14 months out, his recovery is centered almost entirely on the rebuild: navigating escrow funds, an SBA loan, and contractor selection while watching the project progress on-site. He reports his experience with Farmers Insurance has been relatively smooth compared to many neighbors, and attributes this partly to having a different carrier than the majority in his area.

The most challenging aspect of his recovery is financial — not the emotional weight of loss, though he did feel acute despair and anxiety in the immediate aftermath. He describes the recovery workload as a part-time job layered on top of normal life. The biggest systemic gap he identifies is the absence of early, sequenced guidance on the rebuild process: he had to learn contractor selection, permitting timelines, and bid evaluation through trial, error, and a community group that emerged organically from neighbors who shared his home style. He wished a structured crash course had existed from day one. Information came through Zoom meetings over months rather than being consolidated at the outset.

Emotionally, his coping style is practical and forward-facing. He returned to routine quickly, worked as a team with his wife, and avoided dwelling on loss. He repeatedly frames his own situation as better than that of others more severely affected — a comparative orientation that functions as both gratitude and a way of keeping perspective. He does not describe intrusive trauma symptoms but recalls genuine despair and financial anxiety in the early weeks.

His relationship with technology for recovery was basic — internet searches rather than any dedicated app or platform. He is modestly familiar with AI tools through his work but skeptical of the hype, finding the practical uplift modest compared to prior technology.

During the MVP demo, his reactions were most enthusiastic about practical features: AI that could track rebuild steps, draft communications with contractors or lawyers, and allow the community to anonymously compare contractor bids. The contractor price comparison idea was the most animated moment in the demo section. He was more neutral on the emotional support features — the anxiety reduction demo prompted a measured, hedged response rather than enthusiasm or resistance. He was open to being a future tester.

Two patterns stand out. First, his recovery orientation is relentlessly practical and future-focused: he subordinates emotional processing to rebuilding, and technology is only useful when it is actionable. Second, he perceives contractor pricing as exploitative, and this distrust of the commercial ecosystem around disaster recovery feels underserved by existing resources.
